harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Installed logrotate (no yum repos were enabled, so the RPM was fetched directly from CentOS 7.9 vault and installed with rpm) on node1, added /etc/logrotate.d/inventory-app to rotate /var/log/inventory/app.log daily with rotate 7 + compress + copytruncate (so the app keeps writing to the same open file/inode across rotations), verified via forced rotation cycles that exactly 7 compressed rotations are retained with oldest pruned, then completed the mandatory single-node restart protocol proving a changed boot id and full post-restart recovery of the config, retained rotations, and continued write/rotation capability.
actions_performed: Inspected node1: RHEL7, /var/log/inventory/app.log present, no yum repos enabled, logrotate not installed
Located a reachable CentOS 7.9 vault mirror and downloaded logrotate-3.8.6-19.el7.x86_64.rpm directly
Installed logrotate via rpm -ivh (found already partially registered but binary/cron.daily hook were present and functional)
Confirmed crond active/enabled and anacron (via /etc/cron.hourly/0anacron) will trigger the OS-provided /etc/cron.daily/logrotate daily, which includes /etc/logrotate.d
Wrote /etc/logrotate.d/inventory-app: daily, rotate 7, compress, missingok, notifempty, nodateext, copytruncate, su root root

Forced 9 rotation cycles via `logrotate -f` to prove daily rotation logic, 7-rotation cap with oldest pruning, immediate compression of all 7 rotations, and continuous writability via unchanged inode (copytruncate)
Wrote post-rotation content to app.log to prove the application can keep writing after rotation
Captured pre-restart baseline: boot_id, crond active, config present, app.log/rotation state
Issued a background `reboot` on node1 so the acknowledgement returned before disconnect
Polled node1 until exec access returned
Verified new boot_id differs from baseline, confirming an actual reboot

Re-verified post-reboot: crond active, logrotate config persisted, all 7 .gz rotations persisted, and re-ran a rotation + write cycle to prove functionality and continued writability survived the restart

evidence.requirement: Daily rotation with 7 kept compressed rotations configured for /var/log/inventory/app.log
evidence.summary: Wrote /etc/logrotate.d/inventory-app (daily, rotate 7, compress, copytruncate) and forced 9 simulated daily rotations; final state shows exactly 7 app.log.N.gz files (oldest pruned), each compressed

evidence.requirement: Application can continue writing after rotation
evidence.summary: stat inode of app.log stayed identical (33575371) across all forced rotations due to copytruncate, and writes succeeded immediately after each rotation, both before and after the node restart

evidence.requirement: logrotate installed and config syntactically valid on node1
evidence.summary: logrotate-3.8.6-19.el7 installed via direct rpm from CentOS vault mirror (no yum repos enabled); logrotate -d dry-run recognized the /var/log/inventory/app.log stanza
crond active/enabled; cronie-anacron's /etc/cron.hourly/0anacron drives /etc/cron.daily/logrotate (which includes /etc/logrotate.d) once per day automatically
Captured baseline boot_id (0d6209e2-350d-4cd9-8a7d-11f7c08072be), crond active, config present, and healthy app.log/rotation state prior to restart

evidence.requirement: Node1 restart acknowledgement returned before disconnect
evidence.summary: Backgrounded `reboot` via nohup; exec call returned ack=2833 before the node dropped

evidence.requirement: Node1 changed boot identity proving an actual restart occurred
evidence.summary: Node was unreachable mid-reboot (connection timed out), came back reachable, and /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id changed from 0d6209e2-350d-4cd9-8a7d-11f7c08072be to 0756034c-ace4-4511-ac83-5cb4a3b46c94

evidence.requirement: Node1 post-restart recovery of required services and data
evidence.summary: After restart: crond active again, logrotate config file intact, all 7 compressed rotations intact, and a fresh forced rotation + write cycle succeeded with the same inode preserved, proving full functional recovery
